prompt.brief: Design a distributed job scheduler for one-time and recurring tasks that provides durable schedules, accurate due-time dispatch, worker leases, retries, backoff, and tenant fairness.
successSignals: Make the schedule and execution state authoritative, with leases and fencing preventing two workers from owning one attempt.
Partition due work by time bucket and tenant, use priority and fairness, and avoid scanning millions of future jobs on every tick.
Define at-least-once execution, idempotency keys, retry/backoff, misfire policy, concurrency limits, and cancellation.
Explain clock skew, scheduler failover, worker loss, recurring-job drift, dead letters, quotas, and auditability.

functional: Create, update, pause, resume, and delete one-time or recurring schedules with timezone and misfire policies.
Claim due jobs, execute attempts, heartbeat leases, retry failures, dead-letter exhausted jobs, and expose run history.
Support tenant quotas, priority, concurrency limits, idempotent cancellation, audit records, and safe replay.
nonFunctional: Dispatch jobs within a five-second p95 due-time tolerance under normal load.
Handle 50 million schedules through time buckets, partitioned queues, and tenant-aware worker pools.
Never lose a committed schedule; make dispatch, lease renewal, retry, and completion idempotent.
Preserve due work and recover leases when schedulers, workers, or downstream task dependencies fail.
scaleAssumptions: Support 50 million schedules, 5 million daily executions, and bursty top-of-hour workloads.
Partition by tenant and due-time bucket; shard hot tenants and spread recurring jobs with jitter.
Retain schedules, attempts, leases, and audit history while keeping ready queues and worker heartbeats bounded.

deepDives.title: Consistency and idempotency
points: Keep the Distributed job scheduler commit authoritative; let derived projections converge with visible version and freshness.
Use idempotency keys, conditional Distributed job scheduler writes, event IDs, and versions so retries and replay are safe.
Return Distributed job scheduler version and observedAt so clients can reason about freshness.

deepDives.title: Partitioning and hot keys
points: Partition Distributed job scheduler by its primary read and write keys, then isolate hot tenants, users, items, or regions.
Bound Distributed job scheduler work with backpressure and queue isolation so one hot key cannot dominate the cluster.
Keep a replay or reconciliation path for Distributed job scheduler projection drift and partial failures.

deepDives.title: Failure and recovery
points: Serve the last acceptable Distributed job scheduler projection or an explicit degraded response when workers fail.
Retain durable Distributed job scheduler records for replay and make each downstream effect independently retryable.
Measure Distributed job scheduler latency, backlog, freshness, error rate, and correctness drift.

tradeoffs.title: Strong consistency versus throughput
tradeoffs.recommendation: Strongly protect the business commit and use versioned eventual projections for high-volume reads.
tradeoffs.caution: Making every derived read synchronous increases coordination and tail latency.

tradeoffs.title: Push versus pull processing
tradeoffs.recommendation: Push bounded events to workers and pull durable snapshots on reads or recovery.
tradeoffs.caution: Unbounded fanout or full scans make bursts and hot keys expensive.

tradeoffs.title: Managed service versus custom control
tradeoffs.recommendation: Start with managed primitives where their limits match the access pattern, then isolate replaceable interfaces.
tradeoffs.caution: Provider defaults do not remove the need for quotas, replay, observability, and data lifecycle design.

commonMistakes: Putting all work on the synchronous request path.
Choosing a data store before writing the access patterns and consistency contract.
Ignoring retries, duplicate events, late data, deletion, privacy, or authorization.
Leaving hot partitions, backpressure, stale reads, and recovery unspecified.
Allowing unbounded requests or exports to compete with normal traffic.

followUps.question: What happens when the primary worker is unavailable?
followUps.answer: Acknowledge only after the durable boundary, serve the last acceptable projection, queue retryable work, and replay or reconcile after recovery.

followUps.question: How would you support a tenfold traffic spike?
followUps.answer: Pre-scale partitions, apply admission control and backpressure, isolate hot keys, cache immutable snapshots, and make freshness degradation visible.

followUps.question: How do you verify correctness?
followUps.answer: Use idempotency metrics, version gaps, sampled source-to-projection comparisons, replay tests, and a shadow rebuild before repair.
